summary:
Police conduct is the clearest documented danger. In September 2017, national police in the capital detained dozens of LGBT people on dubious charges and beatings were documented; at least 60 people were imprisoned or fined, and the raids formed part of a wave of arrests ahead of an international sporting event. In July 2023, officers raided a private birthday party at which queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of being outed.

A trans woman was murdered in the capital in March 2024, and the police investigation into the killing was inadequate. The response of the authorities is as significant as the violence itself: nothing in the record indicates that the state treats the killing of a trans woman as a matter requiring a serious investigation.

In April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the September 2017 arrests and mistreatment of LGBTI people, a matter the Azerbaijani government had acknowledged in 2019. The judgment addresses state conduct that the authorities themselves conceded had occurred.

Hostile messaging originates in official and state-affiliated media. State-affiliated Real TV aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march demanding access to trans healthcare. Media monitoring by QueeRadar found 77% of 428 analysed pieces hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people, and an activist was told to remove a rainbow flag from a cafe in Baku.

For a visitor, the practical reading is that contact with police carries a risk of mistreatment rather than an expectation of protection, and that visible signs of LGBTI affiliation can attract hostile attention from media and officials in both public and semi-public settings.
tangentialFactors:
Coercion within families sits alongside state conduct as a documented risk. A family forcibly transported an 18-year-old woman to the capital after she came out, an incident recorded in the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025.

Mass arrests have historically clustered around high-profile international events. The September 2017 crackdown preceded the Islamic Solidarity Games, and at least 60 people were imprisoned or fined in the raids, according to contemporaneous reporting by The Guardian and Human Rights Watch.

A shadow report submitted to the CEDAW committee by the Gender & Development Social Union describes state-approved ignorance of LGBTI issues and militant homophobia and transphobia in both official and private media, alongside forced marriages of lesbian, bisexual and trans people. The submission is an NGO account rather than a committee finding.

The ECtHR ruling of April 2024 places Azerbaijan's treatment of LGBTI applicants under supranational review, but the judgment text has not been examined for the scope of any remedies or their implementation.
localsOnly:
Changing identity documents is reported as impossible for trans women, according to the Gender & Development Social Union shadow report to CEDAW. This is a resident-facing barrier with no visitor equivalent, but it shapes what identification trans residents can produce to any authority.

Discrimination has direct economic consequences. Trans people in Azerbaijan are rejected from jobs and housing and pushed into black-market work and precarious housing, an OC Media feature by Ali Malikov reports. The article profiles Durdana, 29, who was arrested, denied housing and employment, and left dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer closed.

The Gender & Development Social Union reports serving more than 200 LBT people, indicating a community support network that operates under constraint rather than an absence of organising altogether.

Forced marriage is documented as a practice affecting lesbian, bisexual and trans women in the same CEDAW shadow report.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources reviewed here do not address whether gender expression or gender identity is criminalised in Azerbaijan, what penalties might apply, or whether any statute regulates public order in ways used against trans people. That question is unresolved on this inventory.

Entry and visa rules, gender markers on passports and other travel documents, and border screening practices are not covered by these sources and remain unsourced.

The outcome of the investigation into the March 2024 murder of a trans woman is not stated in the material reviewed, and whether charges were brought is unresolved.

Access to healthcare, including hormone therapy or gender-affirming care, appears only as the subject of a Women's Day march demand; no source here describes the availability of such care to a visitor.

Hate-crime legislation and its application to anti-trans violence are not addressed in this inventory.
